source.title: Self-Adaptive Training: Bridging Supervised and Self-Supervised Learning
source.authors: Lang Huang; Chao Zhang; Hongyang Zhang

page_placements.theme: Useful internal information can survive corrupted predictions

record.tranche_reason: The study runs ERM on CIFAR-10 data with random label corruption and random input corruptions, reporting training accuracy and generalization behavior.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own ERM results on partially corrupted CIFAR-10 training sets. It does not report ERM results at 100% label corruption. Results cited from other work, including the statement that standard ERM can fit randomized data, are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own ERM training accuracies under random label and input corruption, using corruption schemes from the original work. Its training dynamics also directly test V6, especially Appendix C.2 and Figure 12.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors find that predictions capture useful information early, including under corruption and random continuous supervision, and use this observation to motivate self-adaptive training. Their method improves generalization and representation learning. Their own ERM results also show early learning of correct labels followed by memorization of corrupted labels; complete random categorical-label fitting is cited from prior work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CIFAR10 and ResNet-34 with ERM under partial random label and input corruption; reports training and generalization behavior but does not test fully random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Corruption type and randomization probability; the paper reports different generalization behavior across corruption schemes and noise levels.

fits_no_version.finding: Generalization and clean validation errors under varying fractions of Gaussian or pixel-permuted input corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input corruption changes ERM generalization, with behavior depending on corruption type and fraction.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitting fixed Gaussian real-valued targets yields 57% linear evaluation accuracy, compared with 38% for a randomly initialized network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training against fixed random continuous targets can improve learned representations despite the absence of meaningful label supervision.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The study does not test fully randomized labels. Figure 3 values are not provided in the text, and exact values for the Figure 1 accuracy curves are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. The study's self-adaptive-training results and its cited prior-work findings were not added as rows because the former are not standard ERM and the latter are results from other work.

untested.parts: Completely randomized categorical labels, near-zero training error and chance test performance under that condition, and unchanged hyperparameters relative to true-label training. The random real-valued target experiment reports representation quality rather than categorical label fitting.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across label-corruption fractions.
Training sets consisting entirely of Gaussian images or permuted inputs; exact zero training error rather than the reported nearly perfect accuracy.

The 100% randomization endpoint and chance performance there; perfect training fit at every point of the 0%–90% sweep. The clean validation error trend cannot be recovered from the supplied figure transcription.

Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels; whether removing these regularizers leaves true-label generalization good. The augmentation ablation reports increased errors but does not establish these propositions.
Generality beyond the reported CIFAR10 ERM setting and a direct comparison of wholly true-label versus wholly random-label training.

missing.what: ERM dynamics on untouched and genuinely randomized training examples: correct-label accuracy on randomized examples initially increases and eventually decreases to zero. Add separate rows for the portions and temporal behavior; this directly tests V6.
missing.locator: Figure 12; Appendix C.2, Training accuracy w.r.t. correct labels on different portions of data

missing.what: ERM training accuracy under 80% corruption for each of the four corruption schemes. Figure 11 repeats the accuracy analysis at this higher noise level; the supplied transcription lacks readable curves, so extract values or explicit qualitative states from the figure.
missing.locator: Figure 11a; Appendix C.2, Study on extreme noise

missing.what: Separate the corrupted-label clean validation error curve from the noisy-training/noisy-validation generalization gap. Recover the curve's trend and values, and any available training accuracies across corruption rates, before assessing the full V4 trajectory.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study, so the original-source exclusion does not apply. Remove the record's limits_scope verdicts based solely on untested endpoints. Figure 12 supplies direct V6 evidence that the record incorrectly treats as untested. Exact numerical curve values cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines random label corruption up to 90%, but does not report fitting a completely random labeling of the entire training set or test error at chance.
The study tests Gaussian, random-pixel and shuffled-pixel corruption on a fraction of images, not wholly unstructured inputs across the entire training set.
The study varies random label corruption from 0% to 90%, not all the way to 100%; it reports generalization error and clean validation error, not test error.

rows.measure: Generalization error as corruption rate increases
rows.value: Generalization errors consistently grow as the injected noise level increases; figure only for plotted values.
rows.note: The text describes the increasing trend; exact plotted values are not stated. The sweep stops at 90%.
rows.check: The reported increasing quantity is the accuracy gap between noisy training and noisy validation sets. It does not establish that clean validation error rises steadily toward chance, or that training accuracy remains perfect throughout the sweep. Record the gap trend accurately; extract the separate clean validation curve before assigning a state to the degradation component of V4.
